imageCaption: Aaliyah stands in the farmers market holding a piece of plantain, surrounded by overflowing vegetable stands. Behind her, the same produce appears twice—once in sharp focus, once slightly transparent. Market shoppers move through both versions of reality simultaneously.
text:
The farmers market on Saturday morning was already beautiful before the timeline decided to get involved.

It was the kind of market where the vegetables looked like they'd been grown specifically to make a good impression—deep orange sweet potatoes still wearing flecks of dirt, plantains in various states of ripeness arranged like they were making a musical scale, cilantro in bunches so cheerful they seemed to be actively flourishing in the humid August air.

Aaliyah was holding a piece of plantain—the vendor had let her taste it, had watched her nod, had apparently taken this as a sign that the Gomez family was important—when she noticed that the market was doubling.

Not dramatically. Not in a way that would make people scream or grab their phones. It was subtle enough that at first she thought she was imagining it. The produce stands existed in one version: bright, present, immediate. And then they also existed in another version about thirty seconds behind—slightly transparent, slightly delayed, like the market was watching itself happen.

"Okay," Aaliyah said to no one in particular. "This is new."

Elijah appeared at her shoulder immediately, which meant he'd been tracking her the way Sully tracked interesting smells. "Is this a glitch?"

"Probably," Aaliyah said. She pulled out her phone and started documenting. The glitch was stable—no flickering, no sudden time-skips. Just two versions of the same moment existing in slightly different temporal positions. "The Farmers Market Recursive Loop. It's showing me the market, and then it's showing me what the market looked like five seconds ago."

"Why would it do that?" Elijah asked.

"I have no idea," Aaliyah admitted. "But I'm a scientist and I have a clipboard—well, a phone—so I'm going to gather data."

She walked deeper into the market, watching how the glitch behaved. The two versions moved at the same speed, one trailing the other like an echo. A woman picking up tomatoes existed in both timelines. A child pointing at bright purple cabbages existed in both. Even the sounds came in stereo—the vendor calling out prices, the hum of the neighborhood, the distant sound of a dog barking very much like Sully, which made sense because—

"Sully!" Elijah shouted. "Stop eating the samples!"

Sure enough, Sully had found the vendor station that offered free tastes and had apparently decided that sampling was his primary responsibility as a family member. He was working through various roots and vegetables with the enthusiasm of a dog who'd just discovered his life's purpose.

"That's not helping with the glitch documentation," Aaliyah said, but she was already writing down: *Dog appears to be unaffected by temporal recursion. Continues eating across both timelines simultaneously.*

"Sully understands food more than he understands time," Elijah said this with absolute certainty. "He's probably helping. He's like... glitch seasoning."

"That's not a thing," Aaliyah said.

"Not yet," Elijah agreed. "But give him time. He'll make it a thing."

Luisana and Anthony appeared from the far end of the market, arms full of ingredients. Anthony had the expression of someone who'd gone to get plantains and had instead discovered an entire philosophy about how vegetables could be arranged. Luisana was holding her journal and writing constantly, which meant the glitch had already become a story in her mind.

"It's doubling," Anthony said, not asking. Just observing. "Is the food doubled or is just the space?"

"Both," Aaliyah said. She held up her phone. "The timeline is showing us two versions of the same moment. Recursion. It's not dangerous, it's just... persistent."

"Why would it do that while you're shopping for sancocho?" Luisana asked. She was still writing, her journalist instincts fully activated. "What's the emotional resonance?"

And that was the question that made Aaliyah stop typing notes and actually think about what the glitch was doing.

"It's showing me what I already picked and what I'm about to pick," she said slowly. "It's showing me the past and present versions of the same choice."

"Because you're making a recipe that has to work on multiple Sundays," Luisana said. She looked at the two timelines overlapping. "The glitch is showing you what the sancocho was, and what it will be."

"Or it's just a temporal hiccup," Anthony said cheerfully, but he was smiling like he understood that the timeline was being very helpful. "Either way, we should get back to Marco's before this loops us into September."

They started gathering ingredients with new purpose. Sweet potatoes, plantains, cilantro, garlic, onions, the kind of root vegetables that made sense for a dish that would be different every Sunday but still recognizably itself. Sully completed his tasting mission and reported for duty, bringing with him a piece of carrot that someone had definitely given him, which meant at least one vendor knew to expect dogs to have independent food agendas.

The glitch stayed stable the entire time. The echo of the market followed the actual market. Aaliyah kept documenting because this felt like the kind of glitch that might teach her something about how the resonance frequency worked. The timeline wasn't stopping them from shopping. It was just showing them that every choice they made existed in two states—the choice they were making and the choice they'd made a moment ago.

By the time they left the market, Aaliyah's phone had seventeen notes, a dozen photos, and the beginning of understanding something about how the Cascade worked.

As they walked home with their arms full of ingredients, Elijah asked, "Do you think the glitch knew you needed to see that?"

"The glitch doesn't think," Aaliyah said. "It just... happens."

"But it happened right when we needed it," Elijah pointed out. "Right when you were trying to figure out a recipe that has to exist in multiple versions. That's like, really good timing for something that's supposed to be random."

Aaliyah didn't have an answer to that. She was too busy realizing that Elijah was probably right, which happened more often than she wanted to admit, and which made it harder to explain away the impossible things as coincidence.

The timeline, it seemed, was very interested in helping them build a meal that could last.

And it was showing them exactly how.
